transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, doctor. Thank you. Um, well, what finally pushed me to actually come in is... work. I'm a health services manager, and I can start an EPIC quality report, or, you know, sit down in a clinic metrics meeting with every intention of tracking what's going on. But within just a few minutes, my mind has drifted so far that I’m just rereading the same numbers over and over. 

Which is honestly so frustrating right now because EPIC just had this massive system update, right? And the new dashboard is completely counterintuitive. I was telling my sister about it—she works in healthcare administration too, over at Memorial—and she said her hospital actually refused to update their system because of exactly this issue. We had an IT guy in last week, Greg I think, and he spent half the afternoon just trying to fix the drop-down menus for the nursing staff. He was telling me about his golden retriever having knee surgery, which sounded so expensive... 

Wait, I'm sorry, what was I saying? Oh. Right. The reports. The point is, I'll be looking at these screens or sitting in these metric reviews, and I'll suddenly realize I've completely missed the whole point of the discussion. My brain just goes somewhere else entirely.

You mentioned this happens at work during reports and meetings. Do you notice similar difficulties concentrating or your mind wandering in other situations—like at home, during conversations with friends, or when doing personal tasks?

At home? Um... I'm not really sure. I haven't really thought about it, to be honest. I mean, when I'm at home, I'm mostly just trying to decompress, you know? Like, my husband and I just started watching this new baking competition on Netflix. The one where they make those massive chocolate sculptures? It is just amazing what they can do with modeling chocolate. I actually tried making a layered chocolate cake for my niece's birthday last month—she just turned 12, which is terrifying because I swear she was just a toddler yesterday—and the frosting completely melted everywhere because I didn't let the cake cool long enough. My kitchen was an absolute disaster. My husband had to spend an hour scrubbing the granite... 

But, um, I'm sorry, what were you asking? Oh, right, concentrating. Yeah, I don't know. I haven't really noticed it happening with friends or at home. It's really just the work stuff that's standing out to me right now.
When you're doing something you really enjoy or find interesting—like watching that baking show you mentioned—do you have trouble keeping your attention on it, or does your focus stay pretty good?

Um, well, when I'm watching the baking show, I think I'm pretty focused? I mean, it's really visually engaging. But, you know, it's funny you mention the baking show, because yesterday I was watching an episode where they had to make a croquembouche, and I realized I don't actually own a good piping bag. I bought one from Target a few years ago, but the seams busted the first time I used it. It was a complete mess. I was trying to pipe deviled eggs for Easter dinner—my mother-in-law always insists on having deviled eggs, even though nobody really eats them except her. She has this vintage crystal egg platter that she brings out every single year, and if you don't fill every slot, she gets offended. I swear, the pressure of Easter dinner is worse than the clinic metrics meetings sometimes. We usually have about fifteen people over, and my sister-in-law always brings her famous potato salad, which, honestly, has way too much celery in it... 

Wait, what did you ask me? I'm sorry, I completely lost my train of thought. Oh, right, my focus. Yeah, I think if it's something I really like, I'm okay at paying attention. I haven't really noticed a problem with that.

When you're doing routine tasks that aren't particularly interesting—like paying bills, doing laundry, or organizing things around the house—do you find yourself having trouble staying focused on those activities, or can you usually get through them okay?

Routine tasks? Um, let me think. I mean, laundry is just endless, isn't it? It feels like the minute I empty the basket, it's full again. I actually tried switching to those new laundry detergent sheets because I saw an ad on Facebook about how much plastic waste the big jugs create. The ad had this really sad video of a sea turtle, and I just felt awful. So I bought a six-month supply, but honestly, they don't get the smells out of my husband's gym clothes at all. He plays in this men's recreational basketball league on Tuesday nights, and I swear, the guys on his team take it way too seriously. One of them actually twisted his ankle last week because he tried to dunk—he's like 45, he has no business trying to dunk! They had to call an ambulance and everything, and it caused this huge delay on the court. 

Wait, what was the question? Oh, staying focused on chores. Um, I don't know, I guess I get through them okay? I mean, the house isn't falling apart or anything, so I must be getting them done. I haven't really noticed a huge problem with it.

When you're working on something at work that you find genuinely interesting or important—not just the routine reports—do you notice the same difficulty concentrating, or does your attention stay with it?

Um, interesting things at work... I think I do okay? Like, if we're launching a new patient portal system or something, I get really into it. I actually love looking at the user interface designs. We had this one vendor come in last month to pitch their software, and their sales rep was wearing the most incredible statement necklace. It was this chunky turquoise and silver piece, and I couldn't stop looking at it. I actually collect turquoise jewelry—my grandmother grew up in New Mexico, and she used to send me these little silver rings with turquoise stones for every birthday until I was about eighteen. I have this whole velvet-lined display box for them on my dresser, but honestly, it's getting so dusty because I never remember to wipe it down. Dusting is just the worst chore, isn't it? It just pushes the dirt around into the air, and then my allergies act up, and I'm sneezing for the rest of the afternoon...

I'm sorry, I did it again, didn't I? What were we talking about? Oh, right, interesting work stuff. Yeah, I don't really know if I have trouble with that. I haven't really noticed it being an issue if it's something I actually care about.

I've noticed during our conversation that you tend to go off on tangents—like when I ask about one thing, your mind jumps to related topics, and then you have to ask me what we were talking about. Does that happen to you a lot in everyday conversations, or is it mainly just happening right now in this interview?

Um, everyday conversations? I mean, I guess it happens sometimes? It's just that people will say something, and it reminds me of something else, and then my brain just kind of goes there. Like yesterday, my neighbor was telling me about her new golden retriever puppy, and it made me think of this golden retriever I had growing up named Buster. Buster was the sweetest dog, but he had this terrible habit of chewing on the baseboards. My dad was so mad because we had just moved into that house, and it was a brand new build. He spent hours trying to patch it up with wood filler, but you could always tell. We actually had to hire a contractor eventually, which reminds me, I really need to call the guy about our gutters. They've been overflowing every time it rains, and the water is pooling right next to my hydrangeas. I planted those hydrangeas three years ago, and they're finally starting to bloom that perfect blue color because I've been adding aluminum sulfate to the soil... 

Wait, I'm doing it right now, aren't I? Oh gosh, I'm sorry. Um, yeah, I guess I don't really know if it happens a lot. I haven't really kept track of it. Maybe it does? I'm not totally sure.

When you think back to your school years—elementary, middle, high school—did you have similar problems with staying focused on schoolwork or keeping your attention on things, or is this difficulty with concentration something that's really just started happening more recently?

School years? Oh, wow, that feels like a lifetime ago. Um, yeah, I think it's always been there. Even back in elementary school, I remember my teachers were always writing on my report cards that I was bright but careless. They used that word a lot—careless. And my mother, bless her heart, she used to have to sit with me at the kitchen table every single night while I did my homework. The kitchen table was this big, heavy oak thing that my parents bought at an estate sale before I was born. It had these huge claw feet, and I used to pretend they were dragon claws when I was little. I actually saw a table just like it on an antique appraisal show the other night. I love watching those shows, it's so fascinating what people just have sitting in their attics. This one lady brought in a vase she bought at a garage sale for two dollars, and it turned out to be worth like fifty thousand dollars! Can you imagine? I should really go through the boxes in my garage, but it's so hot in there right now...

Wait, sorry. School. Right. Um, yeah, my mom had to sit with me because I was always losing track of my assignments or I'd forget my books at school. So, no, it's not a new thing. It's pretty much always been like this, I guess.
Do you find yourself fidgeting a lot, feeling restless, or having trouble sitting still? Or do people ever comment that you seem to have a lot of energy or that you're always on the go?

Fidgeting? Um, no, I don't think so. I mean, I don't really have any trouble sitting still. I actually sit at my desk at the clinic for hours at a time without moving much. We just ordered these new ergonomic chairs for the whole administrative team last week because everyone was complaining about lower back pain. Good lumbar support is just so critical, you know? My brother-in-law is a physical therapist, and he is always lecturing us about posture at family dinners. He actually just got back from a conference in Seattle and brought us this amazing coffee from Pike Place Market. I absolutely love a good dark roast, but if I drink it after like, two in the afternoon, I'm just lying awake all night staring at the ceiling. I really need to get better at switching to chamomile tea in the afternoons. I bought this beautiful cast iron teapot just for that, but it's so heavy to lift when it's full of water... 

Wait, I'm doing it again. I am so sorry. What did you ask? Oh, right, being on the go and having a lot of energy. No, nobody's ever told me I have a lot of energy. I'm usually pretty tired by the end of the day, honestly, so I don't really get restless like that.

My brother-in-law is a physical therapist, and he is always lecturing us about posture at family dinners. He actually just got back from a conference in Seattle and brought us this amazing coffee from Pike Place Market. I absolutely love a good dark roast, but if I drink it after like, two in the afternoon, I'm just lying awake all night staring at the ceiling. I really need to get better at switching to chamomile tea in the afternoons. I bought this beautiful cast iron teapot just for that, but it's so heavy to lift when it's full of water... 

Wait, I'm doing it again. I am so sorry. What did you ask? Oh, right, being on the go and having a lot of energy. No, nobody's ever told me I have a lot of energy. I'm usually pretty tired by the end of the day, honestly, so I don't really get restless like that.

inference.note: Ruled out F98.8. Patient demonstrates classic ADHD presentation: lifelong history of inattention (teachers noted 'bright but careless'), significant difficulties with sustained attention on non-preferred tasks (work reports), tangential speech with frequent topic derailment and loss of thread, difficulty with routine tasks, but preserved focus on interesting activities. No evidence of specific learning disorder, speech-language pathology, or motor coordination issues that would suggest F98.8. The pervasive, lifelong pattern and inattentive presentation (without hyperactivity/restlessness) strongly indicates F90.9 (ADHD, predominantly inattentive type).
